title: A first conversation in Spanish
summary: Choose useful greetings, exchange names and close a short conversation, then write your side of a short role-play that a teacher reviews against a rubric. English explanations; no pronunciation score or fluency claim.

objectives.description: Choose a greeting that fits an explicitly stated conversational setting.
Recognize and complete a short name exchange with the stated form of address.
Choose a courtesy or farewell that matches the intended action.
Write your side of a short exchange in a stated setting: greet, give a name, thank and say goodbye.

blocks.markdown:
A greeting opens contact. **Hola** is a useful general hello. It is not tied to a particular hour, and it can stand alone or be followed by a person's name. In writing, you may see **Hola, Ana**: the comma separates the greeting from the name being addressed. You do not need to give a long speech to begin a friendly exchange.

Three common greetings refer to the time of day: **buenos días** for the morning, **buenas tardes** for the afternoon, and **buenas noches** for the evening or night. Use the whole phrase as a small unit. Notice that días goes with buenos, while tardes and noches go with buenas. You can learn those combinations before studying adjective agreement in detail.

A conversation might begin with one person saying “Hola” and the other replying “Hola.” If someone greets you with “Buenos días,” returning “Buenos días” is a normal response. You are responding to a greeting, not being asked to translate each individual word.

Context can make more than one expression reasonable. Hola is still a greeting in the morning, so a question asking for the *time-specific* morning greeting is more precise than a question claiming there is only one possible morning greeting. Our checks state which intention to satisfy. Actual boundaries between afternoon and evening vary across communities and situations; this course does not assign a universal clock time.

Buenas noches can also occur when saying goodnight. Listen to the situation: arriving and greeting someone is different from ending an encounter. The same familiar words can serve a related purpose at another point in the conversation.

Practice a two-line exchange on paper using a made-up name and an explicitly stated time of day. First choose a general greeting, then try a time-specific one. This text course checks recognition and conversational choice, not accent, pronunciation or spoken fluency. No recording or external conversation is required to complete the lesson.

Once a greeting has opened the conversation, you can give your name with **Me llamo...**. For example, “Me llamo Clara” means “My name is Clara.” Treat me llamo as a useful complete pattern. Replace the example name with any name you choose for practice; this course does not need your personal information.

To ask one person their name in the tú form, use **¿Cómo te llamas?** The opening inverted question mark and the closing question mark show where the written question begins and ends. The accent in cómo belongs in this question. In the choice questions, you select a phrase rather than type accents under time pressure.

Here is a short exchange: “Hola. Me llamo Clara. ¿Cómo te llamas?” “Me llamo Pablo.” The answer supplies the requested name. A reply such as “Bien, gracias” answers a different kind of question about how someone is doing; it does not supply a name.

Spanish has different forms of address. **¿Cómo se llama usted?** is an usted-form way to ask the person you are addressing their name. Tú and usted usage varies by region, relationship and setting. We will explicitly tell you when an exercise uses usted; do not infer a universal rule from someone's age, clothing or occupation.

After giving your name in an informal exchange, **¿Y tú?** can return the same question: “And you?” It depends on context. Without the preceding name statement, those two words do not specify what information you want. “Me llamo Pablo. ¿Y tú?” makes the intended next response clear.

**Mucho gusto** is a useful “Nice to meet you” expression after introductions. It is not a substitute for giving a name when one has just been requested. Practice the sequence of purposes: greet, give or ask a name, respond, and acknowledge the introduction. The checks ask you to identify a purpose and complete a fresh exchange, rather than memorize one pair of example names.

A short conversation has several different jobs. **Gracias** expresses thanks. **De nada** is a common response to thanks. **Por favor** belongs with a request. Learning which job a phrase does is more useful than treating all polite expressions as interchangeable.

For example, after someone hands you a pencil you might say “Gracias.” They might reply “De nada.” If you are still asking for the pencil, “Un lápiz, por favor” includes “please” in the request. The point in the exchange matters: requesting an action, thanking someone after it, and responding to thanks are three distinct turns.

Do not try to respond word-for-word to every expression. These phrases often work as conversational routines. A friendly “Gracias” normally invites an acknowledgement, not a second request for the same object. You can choose a short appropriate response without constructing a complicated sentence.

To part, **adiós** is a general goodbye. **Hasta luego** is a common “see you later,” while **hasta mañana** explicitly refers to tomorrow. If an exercise asks you to mention seeing someone tomorrow, hasta mañana supplies that detail. A general goodbye can still be polite; the question is which option expresses the specified meaning.

A complete practice exchange might contain a greeting, a small request, thanks and a farewell. Try arranging those purposes first, then supply phrases you know. There is no need to make every conversation follow one script: a name exchange is useful when meeting someone new but unnecessary every time you borrow a pencil from a friend.

For your own practice, choose a fictional situation and explain in English what each Spanish phrase is doing. Then cover the English explanation and choose the phrase again. The final checks use changed situations and fresh responses. They assess a small set of text-based conversational choices, not general fluency or whether a person would always choose the same wording in real life.

# Role-play: your side of a short exchange

So far each check has asked you to pick one phrase. Real conversations string several turns together, so this episode asks you to **write your own lines** for a short role-play. The other person's opening line is given in Spanish, together with the setting and the time of day. You write three to six short lines in Spanish that a person in your position could say.

A good short exchange usually does four jobs in order. It **greets** in a way that fits the time and setting: *Buenos días* in the morning, *Buenas tardes* in the afternoon or early evening, *Hola* between classmates. It **gives a name** when one is asked for or offered: *Me llamo Ana* or *Soy Ana*. It **thanks** at the point where something was given or done: *Gracias* or *Muchas gracias*. And it **closes**: *Adiós*, *Hasta luego*, or *Hasta mañana* when you will meet again tomorrow. Asking something back, such as *¿Y usted?*, keeps the conversation friendly but is optional here.

Short, correct lines are better than long ones. You do not need accents typed perfectly for the review, but you should use the phrases from earlier episodes rather than word-for-word translations from English.

## How your role-play is reviewed

Your lines are read and decided by a **teacher or course reviewer**; nothing marks them automatically. The reviewer checks each rubric criterion (greeting, name, thanks, farewell and the optional question back) and must **quote your own words** for every criterion they mark as met. A criterion without a quote from your text cannot count. If a required criterion is missing, the role-play is marked not yet met and the review says which part to add.

While the review is pending, the episode stays open. You can work on the second family of questions, which asks you to choose the line that best continues a short dialogue. Passing this episode needs independent success in both families: one reviewed role-play and one dialogue question answered without help. If your first role-play is not yet met, rewriting the same scenario is useful practice but does not count as independent evidence; a fresh scenario from the bank does.

Your written lines are learner records. They are kept with your enrollment, shown only to you and to the staff of this course, and are included when you export or erase your data.

assessments.prompt: Type the Spanish greeting for the afternoon (two words).

grading.explanation: Buenas tardes greets someone in the afternoon.

assessments.prompt: You arrive in the morning and want your greeting to mention that time of day. Choose the best fit.

grading.explanation: Buenos días matches the explicitly stated morning and time-specific intention.

assessments.prompt: Type the one-word general Spanish hello that fits any time of day.

grading.explanation: Hola is the general greeting for any time of day.

assessments.prompt: A new classmate says Hola. You want to return a simple greeting. Choose a response.

options.text: Me llamo is the word for goodbye.

grading.explanation: Returning Hola answers the greeting directly. The other options serve different purposes or are incorrect.

assessments.prompt: Type the Spanish greeting for arriving in the evening (two words).

grading.explanation: Buenas noches greets someone on arrival in the evening.

assessments.prompt: You enter a room in the afternoon and choose a time-specific greeting. Which fits?

grading.explanation: Buenas tardes is the afternoon greeting under the stated setting.

assessments.prompt: A classmate greets you with the general hello. Type the same general greeting back (one word).

grading.explanation: Returning Hola answers a general hello with the same general greeting.

assessments.prompt: You arrive for an evening gathering. Which option is an evening greeting?

grading.explanation: Buenas noches can greet someone in the evening; the context here is arrival.

assessments.prompt: Complete the introduction for the name Inés with the two Spanish words that mean my name is: ___ Inés.

grading.explanation: Me llamo introduces the speaker's name.

assessments.prompt: A person asks ¿Cómo te llamas? Which response supplies a name?

grading.explanation: Me llamo Inés responds with the requested name rather than changing the conversational purpose.

assessments.prompt: Type the two Spanish words you say after exchanging names, meaning nice to meet you.

grading.explanation: Mucho gusto acknowledges meeting someone.

assessments.prompt: This practice scene explicitly uses usted. Choose the name question that matches.

grading.explanation: The prompt fixes usted, so ¿Cómo se llama usted? matches that address form.

assessments.prompt: Introduce yourself as Sol in Spanish: type the two words for my name is, then the name.

grading.explanation: Me llamo followed by the name gives your name.

assessments.prompt: You have just said Me llamo Sol in an informal exchange. Which short question returns the name question?

grading.explanation: ¿Y tú? means And you? and refers back to the name just supplied.

assessments.prompt: Someone says Me llamo Ana. Introduce yourself as Leo the same way.

grading.explanation: Use the same pattern: Me llamo and then your name.

assessments.prompt: Two people have just exchanged names. Which option acknowledges meeting them?

grading.explanation: Mucho gusto acknowledges the introduction with Nice to meet you.

assessments.prompt: Type the usual two-word Spanish reply when someone says Gracias to you.

grading.explanation: De nada is the usual reply to Gracias.

assessments.prompt: A person says Gracias after you help them. Which response fits?

grading.explanation: De nada acknowledges their thanks rather than starting a new introduction or request.

assessments.prompt: Type the two Spanish words that add please to a request.

grading.explanation: Por favor adds please to a request.

assessments.prompt: You are asking for water and want to add please. Which phrase completes Agua, ...?

grading.explanation: Agua, por favor is a short request including please.

assessments.prompt: Type the one Spanish word for thank you.

grading.explanation: Gracias means thank you.

assessments.prompt: You are leaving and want to say See you tomorrow specifically. Which fits?

grading.explanation: Hasta mañana explicitly names tomorrow, matching the stated intention.

assessments.prompt: Someone thanks you for holding the door. Type your two-word Spanish reply.

grading.explanation: De nada answers someone who thanks you.

assessments.prompt: Someone has just helped you find your notebook. You want to thank them. Which phrase fits?

grading.explanation: Gracias expresses the gratitude requested in this situation.

assessments.prompt: It is 10 in the morning at a market stall. The stallholder says: «¡Buenos días! ¿Cómo se llama usted? Es para la lista de pedidos.» Write your side of the exchange in Spanish (three to six short lines): greet, give your name, thank the stallholder for the order and say goodbye.

rubric.description: Opens with a greeting that fits the stated time or setting (for example Buenos días, Buenas tardes or Hola).
Gives a name with Me llamo … or Soy …, or answers the other person's question about the name.
Thanks the other person at a sensible point (Gracias or Muchas gracias).
Closes with a farewell that fits the setting (Adiós, Hasta luego or Hasta mañana).
Asks the other person something back, such as ¿Y usted? or ¿Cómo se llama?

assessments.prompt: «¡Buenas tardes! Me llamo Sofía.» Which reply continues the exchange?

grading.explanation: Returning the greeting and giving your own name answers an introduction; de nada answers thanks, and hasta mañana would end the conversation.

assessments.prompt: It is the evening and you meet a new neighbour on the stairs. She says: «¡Buenas tardes! Soy Marta, la vecina del segundo.» Write your side in Spanish (three to six short lines): greet her, give your name, thank her for introducing herself and say you will see her tomorrow.

assessments.prompt: You have just received your coffee. Which line fits next?

grading.explanation: After receiving something, thanks is the expected turn.

assessments.prompt: It is the afternoon at a library desk. The librarian hands you a card and asks: «¿Su nombre, por favor?» Write your side in Spanish (three to six short lines): greet, give your name, thank the librarian for the card and say goodbye.

assessments.prompt: The shopkeeper says «Gracias, hasta luego.» Which reply closes the exchange politely?

grading.explanation: Returning thanks and a farewell closes the exchange; the other options open new turns.

assessments.prompt: It is the first morning of a language class. Your classmate says: «¡Hola! Me llamo Daniel. ¿Y tú?» Write your side in Spanish (three to six short lines): greet him, give your name, thank him for lending you a pen and say see you later.
